title: David, Bathsheba, and Uriah
summary: While Joab besieges the Ammonite capital, David stays in Jerusalem, sees Bathsheba bathing, sends for her, and sleeps with her. When she tells him she is pregnant, he tries to cover it up by bringing her husband Uriah home from the front, but Uriah refuses to go to his wife while the army is in the field. David then sends Uriah back carrying his own death warrant, arranges his death in battle, and marries Bathsheba; the chapter ends by saying that what David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD.
story: This is the turning point of David's life and of 2 Samuel. Up to now David's story has been one of rising: shepherd boy, giant-killer, fugitive, king, conqueror, the recipient of God's covenant promise (chapter 7). From here the story bends downward. The sword will not depart from his house (12:10), and the chapters that follow tell of rape, murder, rebellion, and civil war within David's own family. The Bible does not hide the greatest king of Israel's worst sin; it tells it slowly and in detail. Bathsheba will become the mother of Solomon, and she appears by implication in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as Uriah's wife: "David was the father of Solomon by Uriah’s wife" (Matthew 1:6).
historical: The chapter continues the Ammonite war of chapter 10. Joab and the army besiege Rabbah, the Ammonite capital east of the Jordan, and fight near its walls. Uriah is called a Hittite. The great Hittite empire of Anatolia had collapsed centuries earlier, but the name was used in the Bible for peoples living in Canaan (Genesis 23) and for groups linked to the later Neo-Hittite states of Syria. Whatever his ancestry, Uriah's name probably means the LORD is my light, and he is listed among David's elite warriors, the Thirty (23:39). Bathsheba's father Eliam is probably the Eliam son of Ahithophel in the same list (23:34), which would make her the granddaughter of David's counselor Ahithophel, who later joins Absalom's revolt. That connection is plausible and often suggested, but the text never spells it out.
cultural:
Spring was campaign season in the ancient Near East, after the winter rains and before the harvest. The opening line sets up the contrast: at the time when kings go to war, this king stays home. Palace roofs were flat and used for walking and sleeping in the cool of the evening, and from the palace on the ridge of Jerusalem David could see into lower courtyards. The note that Bathsheba "had just purified herself from her uncleanness" (verse 4) refers to the washing after menstruation required by the law (Leviticus 15:19-28); it tells the reader she was not already pregnant, so the child can only be David's.

Uriah's refusal to go home reflects a soldier's discipline. Israelite warriors on campaign abstained from sexual relations (compare 1 Samuel 21:5), and the ark itself was with the army. Joab's anticipated rebuke in verses 20-21 recalls the death of Abimelech, killed when a woman dropped a millstone on him from a tower at Thebez (Judges 9:50-54); his name Jerubbesheth is a variant of Gideon's other name, Jerubbaal.
literary: The chapter is told with cold economy, and the verb send (shalach) runs through it like a chain: David sends Joab, sends to inquire, sends messengers, Bathsheba sends word, David sends for Uriah, sends a gift, sends a letter by Uriah's own hand. The man who stays home controls everything by sending. The narrator also uses irony throughout. Uriah, the foreigner, is more loyal to Israel's army and ark than Israel's king; drunk, he is more upright than David sober. Joab's instructions to the messenger show he understands exactly what the king wants. David's reply, which literally asks Joab not to let this thing be evil in his eyes (verse 25), is answered by the narrator's verdict in verse 27: "the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD." That is the first time God is mentioned in the chapter.

outline.t: The army at war, the king at home
David takes Bathsheba, and she conceives
David tries to cover the pregnancy, and Uriah refuses to go home
David marries Bathsheba, and God's verdict

doctrines.note: The chapter traces how sin grows: idleness, a look, a taking, then deception, then murder. Each attempt to hide the first act requires a worse one. It also shows sin's social reach; others die at Rabbah because of the plan to kill one man.

The final sentence is God's verdict. No human court could reach the king, and the chapter is written so that it seems he has escaped. The narrator refuses to let that stand: what is hidden from people is not hidden from God.

Power is shown at its most dangerous. The king who was called to administer justice and righteousness (8:15) uses his authority to take another man's wife and life. Scripture does not make its heroes exceptions to the fallenness of all people.

words.note: Shalach, to send. It occurs twelve times in the chapter. The king who should have gone out to war instead sends others, and his sending brings Bathsheba to his bed and Uriah to his death. The word turns an ordinary verb of royal administration into an image of power abused at a distance.

Raa, to be evil or displeasing. David tells Joab, in effect, not to let the matter be evil in his eyes (verse 25, which the BSB renders upset you). The chapter's last line uses the same root: the thing was evil in the sight of the LORD. The repetition sets David's view against God's.

Laqach, to take. David sent messengers "to get her" (verse 4), literally to take her. Samuel had warned that a king would take (1 Samuel 8:11-17), and Nathan's parable in chapter 12 turns on a rich man who took a poor man's lamb.

christ: Matthew names this episode in the genealogy of Jesus: David was the father of Solomon "by Uriah’s wife" (Matthew 1:6). The phrase keeps Uriah's name and David's sin inside the family line of the Messiah. The Bible does not hide that the kingly line through which Christ came was stained with adultery and murder. That honesty points to the need for a different kind of son of David, one who would not take life to secure himself but lay down his own for others. Psalm 51, which its heading connects with this episode, gives the words of confession that the next chapter will draw from David, and the New Testament holds out the forgiveness David sought as a gift through Christ.

hard.q: Was Bathsheba a willing partner or a victim of the king's power?
hard.a: Readers disagree. Some have seen Bathsheba as complicit, bathing where the king might see and making no protest. Many modern interpreters, and a growing number of evangelical and Jewish commentators, argue that the text places all the responsibility on David: he sees, sends, takes, and lies with her, and she is given no speech except the report of her pregnancy. A woman summoned by the king's messengers had little power to refuse. The narrator is careful in the details: Bathsheba bathes at evening in what was likely her own courtyard, the verbs of action belong to David, and Nathan's parable in chapter 12 casts her as a lamb taken from a poor man, not as a partner in the wrong. God's judgment in 12:7-12 falls on David. The text does not tell us what Bathsheba felt. It clearly holds the king accountable for what he did with his power.

questions: The chapter begins with David at home when he should have been with his army. How do idleness and misplaced responsibility open the door to temptation?
Each of David's attempts to hide his sin made it worse. Why is concealment so dangerous?
Uriah, the outsider, shows more integrity than the king. What does it mean that the Bible so often holds up the faithfulness of outsiders?
